diagrams.title: The main electrolytes in body fluid

labels.answer: Carry electrical signals from nerves to muscles

cloze.text: Water-soluble vitamins (B and C) are not {{c1::stored}} in large amounts, so {{c2::regular intake}} is essential.
cloze.extra: They play diverse roles in metabolism, nerve function and tissue health; several directly affect oral health.

cloze.text: Water-soluble vitamins are less likely to reach toxic levels because they are {{c1::excreted in the urine}}.
Thiamin = vitamin {{c1::B-1}}. It helps {{c2::nervous and cardiovascular}} system function.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: 1 tiny tin can — "tin can" = Thiamin.

cloze.text: Thiamin (B-1) deficiency causes {{c1::beriberi}}, damage to the {{c2::nervous and cardiovascular}} system.
Food sources of thiamin (B-1): {{c1::pork}}, whole grains, fortified cereals, legumes, nuts.
Riboflavin = vitamin {{c1::B-2}}; it is the {{c2::most significant B vitamin for angular cheilitis}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: 2 bright red ribbons — "ribbons" = Riboflavin. Important for many metabolic processes.

cloze.text: Riboflavin (B-2) deficiency: {{c1::glossitis}}, {{c2::angular cheilitis}}, dermatitis, anemia.
Food sources of riboflavin (B-2): {{c1::dairy products}}, leafy green vegetables, fortified cereals, meat.
Niacin = vitamin {{c1::B-3}}; it supports {{c2::energy metabolism}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: 3 nieces — "nieces" = Niacin. Sources: meat, poultry, fish, nuts, legumes, fortified cereals.

cloze.text: Niacin (B-3) deficiency causes {{c1::pellagra}}.
cloze.extra: Pellagra = the 4 Ds (see the basic card).

cloze.text: Pantothenic acid = vitamin {{c1::B-5}}; it functions as {{c2::coenzyme A}}, assisting fatty acid metabolism and synthesis.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: 5 cooking pans — "pans" = Pantothenic. Found widely in foods (meat, whole grains, legumes, eggs, vegetables).

cloze.text: Pantothenic acid (B-5) deficiency is {{c1::rare}} (e.g., fatigue, sleep disturbances, numbness).
Pyridoxine = vitamin {{c1::B-6}}; important for overall metabolism and {{c2::nervous system}} function.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: 6 pointy pyramids — "pyramid" = Pyridoxine. Sources: meat, fish, poultry, potatoes, bananas, fortified cereals.

cloze.text: Pyridoxine (B-6) deficiency: weakness, irritability, {{c1::insomnia}}, dermatitis, anemia, {{c2::angular cheilitis, glossitis}}.
Folate = vitamin {{c1::B-9}}; crucial for {{c2::DNA and protein}} formation.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: 9 falling leaves — "leaf" = Folate. Sources: leafy green vegetables, legumes, fortified grains, liver.

cloze.text: Folate (B-9) deficiency: {{c1::neural tube defects (spina bifida)}} and {{c2::megaloblastic}} anemia.
cloze.extra: Note: cooking can destroy folate.

cloze.text: Cobalamin = vitamin {{c1::B-12}}; it assists {{c2::folate}} metabolism and is vital for DNA and nerve cell function.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: 12 cobras — "cobras" = Cobalamin. Significant oral manifestations in deficiency.

cloze.text: Vitamin B-12 (cobalamin) requires {{c1::intrinsic factor}} for absorption; deficiency leads to {{c2::pernicious}} anemia.
Oral signs of B-12 deficiency: {{c1::glossitis}}, {{c2::hemorrhagic gingiva}}, stomatitis, xerostomia, {{c3::bone loss}}.
cloze.extra: Systemic: depression, memory problems.

cloze.text: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is associated with {{c1::collagen synthesis}} and wound healing, and supports the {{c2::immune}} system.
Food sources of vitamin C: {{c1::citrus fruits}}, tomatoes, cantaloupe, strawberries, mangoes, broccoli.
Vitamin C deficiency = {{c1::scurvy}}: early weakness, fatigue, sore limbs; untreated → decreased red blood cells, {{c2::gum disease}}, hair changes, bleeding from the skin.
cloze.extra: Table row continues on p.302.

cloze.text: Vitamin C toxicity is generally low; high doses can cause diarrhea, upset stomach and {{c1::kidney stones}} (in susceptible individuals).
Minerals are {{c1::inorganic}} nutrients vital for bodily functions, from building bones to regulating fluid balance.
{{c1::Calcium}} is the most abundant mineral in the body.
Besides bones and teeth, calcium is essential for muscle contraction/relaxation, nerve transmission, {{c1::blood clotting}} and immune function.
Calcium cannot be {{c1::synthesized}} by the body and requires {{c2::vitamin D}} for absorption.
Calcium deficiency is linked to {{c1::osteoporosis}} (decreased bone density, including {{c2::alveolar}} bone).
Food sources of calcium: dairy products, {{c1::fish with bones}}, legumes, broccoli.
{{c1::Phosphorus}} is the second most abundant mineral; it aids bone and teeth formation and maintains {{c2::acid-base}} balance.
cloze.extra: Like calcium, it requires vitamin D for absorption. Sources: meat, fish, poultry, eggs, milk, processed foods.

cloze.text: Sodium {{c1::retains water}} in the body and is needed for nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction.
cloze.extra: Sources: table salt, soy sauce.

cloze.text: {{c1::Potassium}} aids muscle contraction and the {{c2::electrical conductivity of the heart}}.
cloze.extra: Sources: meats, milk, fresh fruits and vegetables, whole grains, legumes.

cloze.text: {{c1::Magnesium}} facilitates enzyme operation and assists with muscle {{c2::relaxation}} after contraction.
cloze.extra: Sources: nuts, seeds, legumes, leafy greens, seafood, chocolate, hard drinking water.

cloze.text: {{c1::Chloride}} ensures proper fluid balance and forms {{c2::stomach acid}}.
cloze.extra: Sources: table salt, soy sauce.

cloze.text: {{c1::Sulfur}} is found in protein molecules.
cloze.extra: Sources: meats, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, legumes, nuts.

cloze.text: Microminerals (trace elements) are essential nutrients required in very {{c1::small}} amounts.
Iron is a major component of {{c1::hemoglobin}} in red blood cells, which carries oxygen throughout the body.
cloze.extra: Fun Fact: iron is the tiny vehicle that carries oxygen to every cell, including oral tissues.

cloze.text: Iron is abundant in {{c1::liver}} and not found in {{c2::milk}}.
Iron deficiency → {{c1::iron-deficiency anemia}} (fatigue, weakness); iron toxicity → {{c2::hemochromatosis}} (iron overload damaging organs).
Fluorine helps make teeth resistant to caries by {{c1::hardening the enamel}}.
cloze.extra: Sources: fluoridated water, toothpaste, some seafood, tea.

cloze.text: Fluorine deficiency → increased risk of {{c1::dental caries}}; toxicity → {{c2::fluorosis}} (discoloration or pitting of enamel, occurring during {{c3::tooth development}}).
Iodine is essential for the {{c1::thyroid gland}} to produce hormones.
cloze.extra: Sources: commonly added to table salt; seafood, dairy.

cloze.text: Iodine deficiency → {{c1::goiter}} (enlarged thyroid gland) and hypothyroidism; toxicity → thyroid dysfunction.
Zinc aids {{c1::wound healing}} and immune function.
cloze.extra: Sources: tofu, seafood, red meat, nuts, legumes.

cloze.text: Zinc deficiency → impaired wound healing, {{c1::altered taste}}, immune dysfunction; zinc toxicity → nausea, vomiting, {{c2::copper}} deficiency.
Other trace elements include {{c1::selenium}}, copper, manganese, chromium, molybdenum, nickel, silicon, vanadium and cobalt; they play roles in enzyme function and metabolism.
cloze.extra: Sources vary (whole grains, nuts, seafood, vegetables, organ meats). Deficiencies/toxicities are less common but can be severe.

cloze.text: Water is the main component of the body, making up {{c1::60–80%}} of total body weight.

Functions of water: removes waste and reduces risk of {{c1::kidney stones}}; maintains {{c2::body temperature}}; acts as a {{c3::solvent}} for minerals and vitamins; {{c4::lubricates}} organs and joints.
Recommended water intake is about {{c1::2–3 L}} a day ({{c2::8, 8-ounce}} glasses).
Electrolytes regulate {{c1::nerve and muscle}} function, hydrate the body, balance blood {{c2::acidity}} and pressure, and help rebuild damaged tissue.
cloze.extra: Infographic: electrolytes balance fluids, maintain blood pH, carry electrical signals from nerves to muscles. Fun Fact: Na, K and Mg are vital for nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction.

cloze.text: Good sources of electrolytes are {{c1::fruits and vegetables}}; they are also common in {{c2::sports drinks}}.
Common electrolytes include sodium, potassium, calcium and {{c1::bicarbonate}}.
cloze.extra: The infographic shows Na, Cl, Mg, Ca, K as the main electrolytes in body fluid.

cloze.text: Symptoms of electrolyte imbalance: twitching, weakness and, if unchecked, {{c1::seizures}} and {{c2::heart rhythm disturbances}}.
{{c1::Older adults}} are particularly at risk of electrolyte imbalance.
Plaque formation: {{c1::Streptococcus mutans}} uses dietary {{c2::sucrose}} to produce {{c3::dextran}}, which helps plaque adhere to tooth surfaces.
cloze.extra: Dental hygienists play a crucial role in educating patients about the link between nutrition and caries.

cloze.text: Acid production: S. mutans ferments carbohydrates, producing {{c1::lactic acid}}, which lowers the pH on the tooth surface.
Critical pH for demineralization: average {{c1::5.5}} for enamel and {{c2::6.2–6.7}} for cementum.
cloze.extra: Below it, calcium and phosphate ions dissolve from the tooth → demineralization → eventually a cavity.

cloze.text: Below the critical pH, {{c1::calcium and phosphate}} ions dissolve from the tooth structure.
Many popular energy drinks have a pH often below {{c1::3.0}}, far more acidic than enamel's critical pH.
cloze.extra: Did You Know: high acidity + frequent consumption → caries and erosion.

cloze.text: Advise patients to eat cariogenic foods {{c1::with meals}} rather than as snacks, to limit the {{c2::frequency}} of acid attacks.
Encourage {{c1::rinsing with water}} immediately after cariogenic foods or drinks to help neutralize oral pH.
Eating {{c1::cheese}} at the end of a meal helps raise and neutralize the pH in the mouth.

Recommend {{c1::complex}} carbohydrates (whole grains, most fruits, vegetables, potatoes, corn) over simple ones (table sugar, syrups, sugary drinks, processed juices) because they are less readily {{c2::fermented}} by oral bacteria.
Crunchy, firm-textured foods like raw vegetables mechanically remove {{c1::food debris}} and stimulate {{c2::salivary flow}}.
Sugar alcohols (e.g., {{c1::xylitol}}, sorbitol, mannitol) provide calories but do not promote caries because oral bacteria cannot {{c2::ferment}} them.
cloze.extra: Xylitol in particular actively inhibits cariogenic bacteria.

cloze.text: Non-nutritive sweeteners (e.g., sucralose, aspartame, saccharin) are much sweeter than sucrose, contain {{c1::no calories}}, and do not cause caries.
cloze.extra: Found in sugar-free soft drinks and various foods.

cloze.text: High intake of sugar alcohols in a short time can cause {{c1::diarrhea}}.
cloze.extra: Did You Know: don't eat a whole bag of sugar-free candy in one sitting.

cloze.text: Cariogenicity depends on the {{c1::frequency}}, {{c2::form}} and {{c3::time (sequence)}} of consumption.
Form: {{c1::sticky}} foods are generally more cariogenic than liquids because they stay on tooth surfaces longer.
Time (sequence): cariogenic foods eaten with a meal are better than between meals because {{c1::saliva flow}} is higher during meals.
Xylitol is a naturally occurring substance (xylose) derived from plant sources like {{c1::birch bark}}, beech trees and {{c2::corncobs}}.
Xylitol can be manufactured through {{c1::hydrogenation}} (adding hydrogen).
Xylitol is a "sugar alcohol" by chemical composition, but it is actually a {{c1::carbohydrate}}, not an alcohol.
Sugar alcohols are {{c1::incompletely absorbed}} from the small intestine, so blood glucose levels stay relatively low.
Xylitol is used with {{c1::diabetic}} patients on a low-carbohydrate, low-sugar diet.
Xylitol inhibits {{c1::Streptococcus mutans}} by disrupting its metabolism, reducing its growth, acid production and ability to stick to teeth.
Xylitol reduces acid production, helping maintain a {{c1::neutral}} pH and prevent enamel demineralization.
Xylitol stimulates {{c1::saliva flow}}, useful for patients with {{c2::xerostomia}}.
Xylitol offers anti-cavity benefit for people whose oral bacteria may be resistant to {{c1::fluoride}} or who have limited fluoride exposure.
Xylitol improves {{c1::halitosis}}: it reduces odor-producing bacteria, and saliva washes away {{c2::volatile sulfur compounds}} (VSCs).
Xylitol is commonly found in {{c1::chewing gums}}, mints and toothpastes.
Mouth: {{c1::salivary amylase}} starts breaking down {{c2::polysaccharides}}; protein undergoes {{c3::mechanical}} breakdown only.
Stomach: amylase {{c1::stops}}; {{c2::pepsin}} breaks proteins into polypeptides.
Pancreas: pancreatic amylase breaks polysaccharides into {{c1::disaccharides}}; pancreatic {{c2::lipase}} breaks fats into free fatty acids and {{c3::monoglycerides}}, which are absorbed.
Small intestine: {{c1::lactase, sucrase, maltase}} break disaccharides into monosaccharides ({{c2::glucose, fructose, galactose}}), which are absorbed.
Small intestine: pancreatic enzymes break polypeptides into peptides, and then {{c1::amino acids}} are absorbed.
{{c1::Bile salts}} (from the liver/gallbladder) emulsify fat in the small intestine.
Digestion breaks complex food molecules into smaller components; it begins in the {{c1::mouth}} with mechanical digestion ({{c2::mastication}}).
Most nutrient absorption occurs in the {{c1::small intestine}}; the large intestine primarily absorbs {{c2::water}}.
Stomach pH is {{c1::1–3}} when empty, rising to {{c2::4–5}} with food.
{{c1::Bicarbonate}} neutralizes the mixture as it leaves the stomach; small intestine pH is about {{c2::8}}.
In phenylketonuria (PKU), {{c1::phenylalanine}} builds up because the {{c2::liver}} cannot metabolize this amino acid.
cloze.extra: It damages the nervous system and causes intellectual disability.

cloze.text: Patients with PKU should avoid {{c1::aspartame}}, which contains high levels of phenylalanine.
Marasmus is caused by {{c1::caloric}} deficiency (including insufficient protein); severe {{c2::muscle wasting}} and {{c3::no edema}}.
Marasmus is most common in children under {{c1::2 years}} (typically 6–18 months) in impoverished regions.
Kwashiorkor is caused by severe {{c1::protein}} deficiency with adequate or near-normal caloric intake.
Kwashiorkor symptoms: growth failure, apathy/listlessness, and {{c1::edema}} in the abdomen and legs.
Kwashiorkor is most common in children around {{c1::1–3 years}}, often after {{c2::weaning}}.
{{c1::Rickets}} is softening of the bones caused by the body's inability to absorb calcium; in adults it is called {{c2::osteomalacia}}.
cloze.extra: The body cannot produce calcium; it must be absorbed from food.

cloze.text: Calcium absorption (and so prevention of rickets) depends on {{c1::vitamin D}}.
Bulimia nervosa is a compulsive disorder with cycles of starvation, {{c1::binging}} and {{c2::purging}}.
Individuals with bulimia are typically {{c1::normal weight or slightly overweight}}; often seen in those with stress/low self-esteem.
cloze.extra: Fun Fact: so dental professionals are often the first to spot it — through oral signs.

cloze.text: Calluses on the knuckles from purging in bulimia are called {{c1::Russell's sign}}.
General signs of bulimia: calluses on knuckles, malnutrition, dehydration, {{c1::cardiac dysrhythmias}}.
Perimolysis in bulimia = erosion on the {{c1::maxillary lingual}} surfaces, with {{c2::raised restoration margins}}.
Key oral signs of bulimia: reduced salivary flow, angular cheilitis, xerostomia, perimolysis, caries, oral lesions, palatal trauma, enlarged {{c1::parotid}} gland.
Oral care for bulimia: {{c1::fluoride therapy}} (trays, rinses, varnish), saliva substitutes/sugar-free aids for xerostomia, daily vitamin/mineral supplements.
Anorexia nervosa: {{c1::extreme weight loss}} from self-starvation, excessive exercise, vomiting, laxatives; caused by {{c2::distorted body image}}.
cloze.extra: Common in young women, low self-esteem, perfectionists. Can be fatal.

cloze.text: In anorexia, oral effects come primarily from severe {{c1::malnutrition}}; perimolysis/salivary gland enlargement are less common unless {{c2::purging}} occurs.
Oral care for anorexia: address malnutrition effects (e.g., weakened enamel) and {{c1::collaborate with the medical team}}.
{{c1::Pica}} is the consumption of non-nutritive substances such as soil or glass.
Pica can be related to {{c1::iron}} deficiency (e.g., eating ice cubes).
cloze.extra: Patients may need therapy; dental professionals should look for trauma in the mouth.

cloze.text: Diabetes mellitus is characterized by high blood {{c1::glucose}} levels.
The {{c1::A1C}} level measures how much glucose is on the red blood cells.
A1C target for diabetics: {{c1::7%}} or less (equivalent to eAG {{c2::154}} mg/dl).

cloze.extra: Book's ranges (they overlap; ADA: normal below 5.7%).

cloze.text: Book: normal plasma glucose is {{c1::70–130}} mg/dl before a meal and less than {{c2::180}} mg/dl after a meal.
Diet for diabetes: rich in {{c1::complex carbohydrates and fiber}} to prevent immediate absorption of glucose into the blood.
cloze.extra: Also: weight loss, regular exercise, meals spaced evenly with one or two snacks, avoid high-glucose foods.

cloze.text: Diabetic patients are at increased risk for {{c1::periodontal diseases}} and infections.
Lactose intolerance is a deficiency of the digestive enzyme {{c1::lactase}}.
Lactose intolerance can be {{c1::congenital}} or secondary to intestinal injury such as {{c2::Crohn's disease}}.
cloze.extra: Symptoms: cramps, gas, diarrhea.

cloze.text: Crohn's disease is a chronic {{c1::inflammatory}} disease of the digestive tract (inflammatory bowel disease), not related to allergies.
cloze.extra: Symptoms: abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss; patients can suffer malnutrition and dehydration. Oral ulcers may occur (photo).

cloze.text: Alcoholics tend to consume {{c1::empty calories}} from sweets and fats for energy and satiety; nutritional deficiencies are common.
Alcoholism is one of the most common causes of {{c1::thiamine (B-1)}} deficiency because the liver uses thiamine and {{c2::niacin}} to metabolize alcohol.
{{c1::Folate (B-9)}} deficiency is also commonly seen in alcoholics.
Narrowing and blockage of blood vessel walls from fatty buildup is called {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
For cardiovascular disease, limit saturated fats and {{c1::LDL}} and increase {{c2::HDL}}.
A common side effect of cardiovascular medications is {{c1::xerostomia}}.
Patients in chemotherapy and radiation therapy need {{c1::more}} nutrients because the body must replace destroyed cells.
cloze.extra: Side effects: nausea, loss of appetite, xerostomia, stomatitis.

cloze.text: After vomiting, cancer patients should rinse with water or {{c1::sodium bicarbonate}} to raise the oral pH before brushing or flossing.
Cancer-therapy home care: keep hydrated (spray water, suck on {{c1::ice chips}}) and avoid {{c2::spicy, salty, hot and sharp}} foods that irritate tissues.

Nutritional counseling by hygienists mostly involves maintaining a healthy oral cavity, e.g., explaining that carbohydrates are fermented by bacteria into {{c1::lactic acid}}, which demineralizes teeth.
Hygienists can detect serious systemic nutritional problems such as bulimia and {{c1::refer}} the patient (dietitian, psychologist, etc.).
A {{c1::food diary}} records all meals, snacks, drinks and supplements for a designated period.
A 24-hour food diary is not representative of the normal diet; {{c1::3-, 5- or 7-day}} diaries are most used.
BMI evaluates weight in relation to height; formula = {{c1::kg/m²}}.
BMI ranges: normal {{c1::18.5–24.9}}; overweight {{c2::25–29.9}}.
BMI ranges: obesity I {{c1::30–34.9}}; obesity II {{c2::35–39.9}}; extreme obesity {{c3::>40}}.
{{c1::Waist circumference}} is a more accurate method for determining obesity than BMI.
BMR (basal metabolism requirement) represents {{c1::60–70%}} of the total energy used by the body at rest.
General daily calorie guidelines: men {{c1::2000–3000}} calories/day; women {{c2::1600–2400}} calories/day.

basic.front: Pellagra (niacin / B-3 deficiency) is characterized by the "4 Ds". Name them.
Why is B-12 deficiency common in strict vegetarians?
basic.back: Cobalamin is found only in animal products (meat, fish, poultry, eggs, dairy).

basic.front: Why do dentists often recommend vitamin C after periodontal surgery?
basic.back: Vitamin C is essential for synthesizing collagen, a protein vital for wound healing and healthy gum tissue.
A substance that conducts electricity when dissolved in water

basic.front: Why does frequent snacking on sugary/carbohydrate-rich foods raise caries risk?
basic.back: It causes almost continuous acid attacks; saliva cannot fully neutralize the acid or penetrate the plaque between exposures.

basic.front: Board Alert: does xylitol remineralize teeth?
basic.back: No — it PROMOTES remineralization indirectly: stimulated saliva delivers calcium and phosphate. It does not bind to tooth surfaces and strengthen teeth like fluoride.
basic.extra: One word ("promotes") changes everything on the board exam.

basic.back: Purging by insulin-dependent diabetics for sugar (weight) control

basic.front: What must a patient with bulimia NOT do immediately after vomiting?
basic.back: Brush or floss — rinse instead (water or sodium bicarbonate) to raise the pH first.
basic.extra: The rinse advice is from the cancer-therapy home care (p.307).

basic.front: Why check a diabetic patient's blood sugar before long or invasive appointments?
basic.back: To prevent hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia during treatment.

basic.front: What is the main limitation of BMI?
basic.back: It does not differentiate between lean mass and fat.
The nutrient level sufficient to meet the requirements of nearly all healthy individuals
An updated version of the RDA that aims to prevent nutrient insufficiency
The appropriate nutrient intake for healthy people when an RDA is not available
The highest level of nutrient intake that does not pose any risk of adverse health effects

typein.question: What percentage of the body's calcium is stored in bones and teeth? (number + %)
According to the book, restrict sodium intake to how many grams per day?
typein.extra: Sodium can aggravate existing high blood pressure.

typein.question: The body can survive up to how many days without water?
Xylitol has about what percentage fewer calories than table sugar? (number + %)
typein.extra: Yet it is equally sweet or sweeter than sucrose.

typein.question: How many kcal per gram does alcohol provide?

mcq.question: A patient who lacks intrinsic factor presents with glossitis, hemorrhagic gingiva and memory problems. Which vitamin is most likely deficient?
mcq.explanation: B-12 requires intrinsic factor for absorption; deficiency gives pernicious anemia with glossitis, hemorrhagic gingiva and memory problems. Folate deficiency also causes anemia (megaloblastic) but does not depend on intrinsic factor.

mcq.question: A patient taking very high doses of vitamin C for months is at increased risk for which problem?
mcq.explanation: High-dose vitamin C can cause diarrhea, upset stomach and kidney stones. Hemochromatosis is iron overload, not vitamin C toxicity.

mcq.question: A patient with hypertension asks which mineral to limit. Which should the hygienist identify?
mcq.explanation: Sodium retains water and can aggravate existing high blood pressure (book: restrict to 3 g/day). Potassium is not restricted; it aids muscle contraction and heart conductivity.

mcq.question: A patient with iron-deficiency anemia asks for food advice. Which food is NOT a source of iron according to the book?
mcq.explanation: The book says iron is abundant in liver and not found in milk. Liver is the richest source listed, so it is the best distractor.

mcq.question: A patient sips one can of regular soda slowly over the whole afternoon. Which cariogenicity factor makes this habit especially harmful?
mcq.explanation: Sipping prolongs and repeats acid exposure — frequency. Drinking it all at once is less harmful. Form would apply to sticky vs liquid foods; a liquid is the less cariogenic form.

mcq.question: Which recommendation is most appropriate for a patient who refuses to give up candy?
options: A. Eat it between meals so it does not mix with food
B. Eat it with meals and rinse with water afterwards
C. Switch to processed fruit juice
D. Eat it slowly over several hours
mcq.answer: B. Eat it with meals and rinse with water afterwards
mcq.explanation: Cariogenic foods with meals (higher saliva flow) limit acid attacks; rinsing with water helps neutralize pH. Processed fruit juice is a simple carbohydrate and still cariogenic.

mcq.question: Which statement about xylitol is most accurate?
options: A. It remineralizes teeth by binding to enamel like fluoride
B. It promotes remineralization by stimulating saliva flow
C. It is slowly fermented by S. mutans to a weak acid
D. It is a true alcohol and should be avoided in recovering alcoholics
mcq.answer: B. It promotes remineralization by stimulating saliva flow
mcq.explanation: Xylitol promotes remineralization indirectly (saliva delivers calcium and phosphate); it does not bind to teeth like fluoride. Oral bacteria cannot ferment it, and it is a carbohydrate, not an alcohol.

mcq.question: Where does chemical digestion of protein begin?
mcq.explanation: In the mouth protein is only mechanically broken down; pepsin in the stomach starts chemical digestion (proteins → polypeptides). The small intestine finishes it (peptides → amino acids).

mcq.question: A normal-weight 22-year-old woman has smooth erosion of the maxillary lingual surfaces, raised amalgam margins, enlarged parotid glands and calluses on her knuckles. What is the most likely condition?
mcq.explanation: Normal weight + perimolysis + parotid enlargement + Russell's sign = bulimia. In anorexia the patient has extreme weight loss and perimolysis is uncommon unless purging occurs.

mcq.question: A diabetic patient's A1C is 6.1%. Based on the book's ranges, this falls in which category?
options: A. Within the diabetic target and in the prediabetes range
mcq.answer: A. Within the diabetic target and in the prediabetes range
mcq.explanation: Target for diabetics is 7% or less; 5.7–6.4% is the prediabetes range, so 6.1% is within target and in the prediabetes band. Above-target would be >7%.

mcq.question: A patient's BMI is 32. How is this classified?
mcq.explanation: Obesity I = 30–34.9. Overweight is 25–29.9; Obesity II is 35–39.9.

mcq.question: A deficiency of which vitamin is most likely to cause delayed wound healing and weakened immune response in the oral cavity?
mcq.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen synthesis, leading to delayed healing and increased susceptibility to infection.

mcq.question: Which macronutrient is essential for tissue repair and immune function, directly impacting periodontal health?
mcq.explanation: Proteins provide amino acids necessary for repair, enzyme production, and immune defense in periodontal tissues.

mcq.question: Which vitamin deficiency can cause glossitis, cheilitis, and angular stomatitis?
mcq.explanation: Riboflavin deficiency leads to mucosal inflammation, causing painful tongue and lip lesions.

mcq.question: Deficiency of which vitamin affects calcium absorption and can lead to defective enamel and bone formation?
mcq.explanation: Vitamin D regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism, critical for mineralization of teeth and bones.

mcq.question: Deficiency in which vitamin can lead to increased susceptibility to oral infections due to its role in immune function?
mcq.explanation: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting immune cells and oral tissues from oxidative damage.

mcq.question: Which carbohydrate is a disaccharide composed of glucose and galactose, found in milk?
mcq.explanation: Lactose is the sugar in milk composed of glucose and galactose; it is less cariogenic than sucrose.

mcq.question: Glycogen is best described as:
options: A. A disaccharide stored in plants
B. A polysaccharide stored in the liver and muscles for energy
C. A fatty acid used for long-term energy storage
D. A protein involved in muscle repair
mcq.answer: B. A polysaccharide stored in the liver and muscles for energy
mcq.explanation: Glycogen is a branched polysaccharide stored mainly in the liver and muscles and serves as a rapid source of glucose for energy.

mcq.question: Which is a characteristic of unsaturated fatty acids?
options: A. They have no double bonds and are solid at room temperature
B. They are saturated with hydrogen atoms
C. They contain one or more double bonds and are typically liquid at room temperature
D. They are always harmful to cardiovascular health
mcq.answer: C. They contain one or more double bonds and are typically liquid at room temperature
mcq.explanation: Unsaturated fatty acids contain one (monounsaturated) or more (polyunsaturated) double bonds, making them typically liquid at room temperature and healthier fats.

mcq.question: Which nutritional deficiency is most commonly associated with the oral condition called "angular cheilitis"?
mcq.explanation: Angular cheilitis often results from deficiencies in iron or B-complex vitamins, leading to inflammation and cracking at the corners of the mouth.

mcq.question: A vegan patient presents with aphthous ulcers, burning tongue, and glossitis. These oral symptoms are often associated with which nutritional deficiency?
mcq.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurological symptoms and mucosal changes like glossitis and burning sensations. B12 is only obtained through animal sources, so vegans and vegetarians may be deficient if they are not supplementing B12.

mcq.question: Which method is considered a more accurate way to determine obesity compared to Body Mass Index (BMI)?
mcq.explanation: Waist circumference is considered a more accurate method of determining obesity than BMI, as BMI does not differentiate between lean mass and fat.

mcq.question: Which fat-soluble vitamin, when consumed in excessive amounts, is known to interfere with blood coagulation?
mcq.explanation: Vitamin E can act as an anticoagulant and interfere with blood coagulation, especially at high doses.

mcq.question: In which part of the digestive system does the significant breakdown of large fat droplets into smaller ones, aided by bile salts, primarily occur?
mcq.explanation: In the small intestine, bile salts break down large fat droplets into smaller droplets, which are then further digested by pancreatic lipase.

mcq.question: Which two minerals are most abundant in the body and work together with Vitamin D to promote the mineralization of teeth and bones?
mcq.explanation: Calcium and phosphorus are the most abundant minerals in the body, and both are essential for the formation and mineralization of bones and teeth, with vitamin D crucial for their absorption.

mcq.question: A vegetarian patient carefully combines rice with beans in their meal. This is an example of consuming what type of proteins to ensure adequate nutrient intake?
mcq.explanation: Complementary proteins are incomplete proteins that, when combined (like rice and beans), provide all essential amino acids that the body needs.
